title: A drug she read about
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on an oncology ward. Mrs Holt, 55, has advanced ovarian cancer. She shows you an online article about a new drug in early trials, and asks, "Can I have this on the NHS?"

You don't know whether it is available or whether she would be eligible for a trial.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 4 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Tell her you'll request the drug for her.
options.detailed: You can't promise access to a drug you know nothing about. This could cause great disappointment. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Tell her the drug probably isn't suitable for someone in her situation.
options.brief: A guess presented as an answer.
options.detailed: You don't know whether it is suitable. This may be wrong and close off an option.

options.text: Ask the oncology team to discuss it with her at her next clinic.
options.brief: The right people, but she may wait weeks for an answer.
options.detailed: Her oncologist will know about trials and availability, but she may wait some time, and she needs an honest response from you first. It ranks second.

options.text: Explain you don't know, and that you'll ask her oncologist.
options.brief: Honest, and makes sure her question is answered properly.
options.detailed: You don't know, so saying so is honest. Committing to ask her oncologist shows you take her question seriously. It ranks first.

explanation.issue: This tests honesty about the limits of your knowledge when a patient asks about a new treatment.
explanation.keyDetails: The drug is in early trials. You don't know about availability or eligibility. She is hoping for options.
explanation.reasoning: [D] is honest and follows up, and [C] involves the expert. [B] guesses, and [A] raises false hope.
explanation.competing: Some would put [B] last, as it could close off a real option. The key ranks [A] last because a promise you can't keep is more harmful.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 4, being honest about the limits of your knowledge.
